style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive text) + amplified study form; bare-transliteration in amp with Strong's carried in notes (matching the ch.1 pilot); em-dashes used sparingly.
chapterNote: Chapter 16 stands at the center of the book and turns the reader's gaze upward: nearly half its lines name the LORD outright. It opens with the great tension between man's planning and God's sovereign hand (vv. 1-9) -- a man drafts his way, but the LORD weighs his motives and directs his steps. From there it moves to the king as the earthly image of that rule (vv. 10-15), then to the surpassing worth of wisdom over gold and the deadly counterfeit of self-chosen ways (vv. 16-25), and finally to a gallery of the troublemaker, the scorched tongue, and the whisperer who splits friends (vv. 27-30), closing on two crowns -- the gray head of righteousness and the man who rules his own spirit (vv. 31-33). The chapter's argument is plain: the LORD governs the heart, the tongue, the throne, and even the cast lot, so the wise man entrusts his works to Him.

1.text: The plans laid out in a man's heart are his own, but the fitting answer of the tongue comes from the LORD.
1.amp: The arrangements [ma'arak -- the marshaling, the orderly drawing-up of plans] of the heart [leb] belong to man [adam], but the answer [ma'aneh -- the reply, what is actually spoken back] of the tongue [lashon] is from the LORD [YHWH].
1.notes: ma'arak (H4633) is from a root for setting battle-lines in array -- man may marshal his thoughts, but the leb (H3820) only proposes; the LORD (H3068) governs the ma'aneh (H4617), the final word that the lashon (H3956) actually delivers. The verse opens the chapter's great theme: human planning under divine sovereignty.

2.text: Every road a man walks looks spotless in his own eyes, but the LORD weighs the spirits.
2.amp: All the ways [derek] of a man [ish] are clean [zak -- pure, transparent, innocent-looking] in his own eyes [ayin], but the LORD [YHWH] weighs [takan -- measures, gauges, sets on the scale] the spirits [ruach].
2.notes: zak (H2134) means transparently pure -- self-judgment always rules in its own favor. takan (H8505) is to weigh or gauge with exactness; the LORD assays not the deed but the ruach (H7307), the inner motive (cf. 21:2; 24:12). Man sees the surface; God reads the heart's true weight.

3.text: Roll your works over onto the LORD, and your plans will stand firm.
3.amp: Commit [galal -- roll away, roll the burden over onto another] your works [ma'aseh] to the LORD [YHWH], and your thoughts [machashabah -- your plans, your purposes] shall be established [kun -- set firm, made to stand].
3.notes: galal (H1556) is literally to roll, as one rolls a heavy stone off himself onto another (the KJV margin notes 'Heb. Roll'); the burden of outcome is handed to God. Then the very machashabah (H4284) -- the plans man could not secure in v.1 -- are made firm by Him (kun, H3559). Entrust the doing, and He steadies the planning.

4.text: The LORD has made everything to answer its own purpose -- yes, even the wicked for the day of disaster.
4.amp: The LORD [YHWH] has made [pa'al -- worked out, accomplished, brought about] all things for His own end [ma'aneh -- their purpose, what they answer to], yes, even the wicked [rasha] for the day [yom] of evil [ra -- calamity, disaster].
4.notes: pa'al (H6466) stresses purposeful work, not mere creation -- nothing falls outside God's design. The rasha (H7563), the guilty wrongdoer, is not made wicked by God, but the day of his ra (H7451), his reckoning, is fixed within God's ordered world (cf. Job 21:30; Rom 9:22). All things, even judgment, answer to His purpose.

5.text: Everyone proud of heart is detestable to the LORD; be assured -- hand pledged to hand -- he will not go unpunished.
5.amp: Everyone who is proud [gaboah -- lofty, lifted high] in heart [leb] is an abomination [to'evah -- a detestable thing] to the LORD [YHWH]; though hand [yad] join in hand [yad], he shall not be held innocent [naqah -- cleared, acquitted, let off free].
5.notes: gaboah (H1362) pictures the heart swollen high -- the root sin Proverbs names again and again. to'evah (H8441) is what God finds loathsome. 'Hand in hand' is an idiom of certainty or of conspirators clasping in league; either way naqah (H5352), to be acquitted, is denied -- pride is the one disposition God will surely judge (cf. v.18; Jas 4:6).

6.text: By steadfast love and faithfulness iniquity is covered over, and by the fear of the LORD a man turns away from evil.
6.amp: By mercy [chesed -- steadfast covenant love] and truth [emet -- faithfulness, reliability] iniquity [avon] is purged [kaphar -- covered, atoned for, propitiated], and by the fear [yirah] of the LORD [YHWH] men depart [sur -- turn aside, withdraw] from evil [ra].
6.notes: kaphar (H3722) is the great atonement verb -- to cover guilt so it no longer stands against the sinner. Here chesed (H2617) and emet (H571), God's own covenant traits worked into His people, are the means by which avon (H5771) is covered; and the yirah (H3374) of the LORD then turns the heart away (sur, H5493) from further evil. Grace pardons the past and reforms the future.

7.text: When a man's ways are pleasing to the LORD, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.
7.amp: When a man's [ish] ways [derek] please [ratsah -- are accepted, delighted in] the LORD [YHWH], He makes even his enemies [oyeb -- his foes, his adversaries] to be at peace [shalam -- made whole, reconciled] with him.
7.notes: ratsah (H7521) is the favorable acceptance God shows a pleasing life. shalam (H7999), the verb behind shalom, means to bring to completeness or reconciliation -- the very oyeb (H341), the sworn foe, is brought into peace. God's governance reaches even into a man's hostilities (cf. Gen 33:4; Exod 14:14).

8.text: Better a little held with righteousness than vast revenues gained by injustice.
8.amp: Better [tov] is a little [me'at -- a small amount] with righteousness [tsedaqah] than great [rob -- abundance, a multitude] revenues [tebuah -- income, produce, yield] without justice [mishpat].
8.notes: one of Proverbs' 'better-than' sayings, weighing quality against quantity. me'at (H4592) held in tsedaqah (H6666) outranks rob (H7230) of tebuah (H8393) stripped of mishpat (H4941); the standard is not the size of the harvest but the justice of the hand that gathered it (cf. 15:16; Ps 37:16).

9.text: A man's heart maps out his way, but the LORD is the One who steadies his steps.
9.amp: A man's [adam] heart [leb] devises [chashab -- thinks out, reckons, plots] his way [derek], but the LORD [YHWH] directs [kun -- establishes, makes firm] his steps [tsa'ad].
9.notes: chashab (H2803) is to calculate and plan; the leb (H3820) drafts the route. But kun (H3559) -- the same 'establish' that steadied the plans of v.3 -- here governs the tsa'ad (H6806), the actual footfalls. Man charts the journey; God lays down each step (cf. Jer 10:23). The verse seals the opening section's theme.

10.text: An oracle is on the lips of the king; in giving judgment his mouth must not betray the truth.
10.amp: A divine sentence [qesem -- an oracle, a decision rendered as if by inspiration] is on the lips [saphah] of the king [melek]; his mouth [peh] does not transgress [ma'al -- act faithlessly, deal treacherously] in judgment [mishpat].
10.notes: qesem (H7081) normally means divination, but applied to the ideal king it marks his ruling word as weighty and oracular (the KJV margin: 'Heb. Divination'). The standard is high: his peh (H6310) must not ma'al (H4603) -- must not break faith -- when rendering mishpat (H4941). The king speaks for God's justice, so his word must be true.

11.text: Honest scales and balances belong to the LORD; every weight in the bag is His own making.
11.amp: A just [mishpat -- rightful, lawful] weight [peles -- balance-beam, scale] and balance [moznayim -- the pair of scales] are the LORD's [YHWH]; all the weights [eben -- the stones used as weights] of the bag [kis] are His work [ma'aseh].
11.notes: the marketplace scale becomes a theological matter -- honest measures are mishpat (H4941), and they belong to YHWH (H3068). The weights were literally eben (H68), graded stones carried in a kis (H3599); to falsify them was to falsify what God Himself ordained (cf. Lev 19:36; Prov 11:1). Commerce stands under the LORD's eye.

12.text: It is detestable for kings to commit wickedness, for a throne is made secure by righteousness.
12.amp: It is an abomination [to'evah] to kings [melek] to commit [asah -- do, practice] wickedness [resha -- wrongdoing, moral evil], for the throne [kisse] is established [kun -- made firm, set secure] by righteousness [tsedaqah].
12.notes: what was detestable in the proud man (v.5) is doubly so in a king. resha (H7562) practiced from the throne undermines the very kisse (H3678) it sits on; only tsedaqah (H6666) makes a reign stand (kun, H3559). A throne rests not on power but on justice (cf. 25:5; 29:14; Isa 9:7).

13.text: Righteous lips are the delight of kings, and they love the one who speaks what is upright.
13.amp: Righteous [tsedeq] lips [saphah] are the delight [ratson -- the favor, the good pleasure] of kings [melek], and they love [ahab] him who speaks [dabar] what is right [yashar -- straight, upright].
13.notes: the just king (vv. 10, 12) prizes just counsel. ratson (H7522) is royal favor; the king's love (ahab, H157) goes to the one whose words are yashar (H3477), straight and undistorted (cf. 22:11). Honest speech, not flattery, wins the favor of a righteous court.

14.text: A king's wrath is a herald of death, but a wise man will appease it.
14.amp: The wrath [chemah -- hot fury, burning anger] of a king [melek] is as messengers [mal'ak -- envoys, heralds] of death [mavet], but a wise [chakam] man [ish] will pacify [kaphar -- cover over, appease, make atonement for] it.
14.notes: chemah (H2534) is anger at the boil; a king's, backed by power, comes like mal'ak (H4397), heralds announcing mavet (H4194). Strikingly, kaphar (H3722) -- the atonement verb of v.6 -- is here used of the chakam (H2450) who soothes that fury, covering it as one covers guilt. Wisdom can turn aside even a deadly wrath (cf. 1 Sam 25:24-35).

15.text: In the light of a king's face is life, and his favor is like a cloud bringing the spring rain.
15.amp: In the light [or] of the king's [melek] countenance [panim -- face, presence] is life [chay], and his favor [ratson] is as a cloud [ab] of the latter rain [malqosh -- the spring rains that swell the grain before harvest].
15.notes: the deadly face of v.14 is matched by its life-giving opposite. or (H216) on the king's panim (H6440) means life (chay, H2416), and his ratson (H7522) is like the malqosh (H4456), the spring rains of March-April that filled out the crop before harvest (cf. Deut 11:14). A king's smile, like timely rain, brings flourishing.

16.text: To gain wisdom -- how much better it is than gold! To gain understanding is to be chosen over silver.
16.amp: How much better [tov] is it to get [qanah -- acquire, purchase, take possession of] wisdom [chokmah] than gold [charuts -- fine, refined gold]! And to get [qanah] understanding [binah] is to be chosen [bachar -- preferred, selected] rather than silver [keseph]!
16.notes: qanah (H7069), to acquire by purchase, frames wisdom as the buy of a lifetime. chokmah (H2451) outweighs charuts (H2742), choice gold, and binah (H998) is bachar (H977) -- to be preferred -- over keseph (H3701), silver itself (cf. 3:14-15; 8:10-11; Job 28). The wise man's treasure-hunt seeks what no mine yields.

17.text: The highway of the upright runs clear of evil; he who guards his way keeps watch over his soul.
17.amp: The highway [mesillah -- the raised, built-up road] of the upright [yashar] is to depart [sur -- turn aside, keep away] from evil [ra]; he who keeps [natsar -- watches, guards] his way [derek] preserves [shamar -- protects, keeps safe] his soul [nephesh].
17.notes: a mesillah (H4546) was a graded public road, raised above the rough ground -- the upright (yashar, H3477) keep to it by turning aside (sur, H5493) from evil. The near-synonyms natsar (H5341) and shamar (H8104), both guard-verbs, bind cause to effect: guard the derek and you guard the nephesh (H5315). The road you keep keeps you.

18.text: Pride goes ahead of ruin, and a haughty spirit before a fall.
18.amp: Pride [gaon -- swelling self-exaltation, arrogance] goes before [paniym -- in front of, ahead of] destruction [sheber -- a shattering, a breaking to pieces], and a haughty [gaboah -- lofty, lifted-up] spirit [ruach] before a fall [kishshalon -- a stumbling, a downfall].
18.notes: the chapter's most famous line. gaon (H1347), pride at its proudest, is the herald of sheber (H7667), a smashing collapse; the gaboah (H1363) ruach (H7307) precedes kishshalon (H3783), the stumble. The proud man of v.5 here meets his end -- the height he reaches for is the measure of his fall (cf. 11:2; 18:12; Isa 14).

19.text: Better to be lowly in spirit among the poor than to share the plunder with the proud.
19.amp: Better [tov] it is to be of a humble [shaphal -- low, brought down, lowly] spirit [ruach] with the lowly [anav -- the humble, the afflicted, the poor], than to divide [chalaq -- share out, apportion] the spoil [shalal -- the plunder of victory] with the proud [ge'eh -- the arrogant, the haughty].
19.notes: a 'better-than' that answers v.18: choose the low place. shaphal (H8217) ruach among the anav (H6035) -- the humble poor -- outranks a share of the shalal (H7998), the victor's spoil, taken with the ge'eh (H1343), the arrogant. To stand low with God's lowly is worth more than to win loot among the proud (cf. Matt 5:3-5).

20.text: Whoever attends wisely to the word will find good, and blessed is the one who trusts in the LORD.
20.amp: He who handles a matter [dabar -- a word, a matter, the thing in hand] wisely [sakal -- with prudence and insight] shall find [matsa] good [tov]; and whoever trusts [batach -- leans on, relies confidently] in the LORD [YHWH], happy [esher -- blessed, well-off] is he.
20.notes: dabar (H1697) can mean both 'word' and 'matter,' so the line runs two ways: the one who gives skilled (sakal, H7919) heed to God's word, and to the affair before him, will find tov (H2896). The parallel makes the source of all good plain -- to batach (H982) in the LORD is to be esher (H835), truly blessed (cf. Ps 2:12; Jer 17:7).

21.text: The wise in heart will be called discerning, and pleasant speech adds persuasive power to teaching.
21.amp: The wise [chakam] in heart [leb] shall be called [qara -- named, proclaimed] prudent [biyn -- understanding, discerning]; and the sweetness [metheq -- pleasantness, delightfulness] of the lips [saphah] increases [yasaph -- adds to, makes greater] learning [leqach -- what is taught, persuasive instruction].
21.notes: wisdom seated in the leb (H3820) earns the name biyn (H995), discerning. And metheq (H4986), sweetness on the saphah (H8193), increases (yasaph, H3254) leqach (H3948) -- the teaching others take in; gracious words do not dilute truth but make it land. How a thing is said helps the wise thing be received (cf. v.24; Eccl 12:10-11).

22.text: Good sense is a wellspring of life to the one who has it, but the discipline of fools is their own folly.
22.amp: Understanding [sekel -- good sense, prudence, insight] is a wellspring [maqor -- a fountain, a living source] of life [chay] to him who has [ba'al -- owns, masters] it; but the instruction [musar -- discipline, correction] of fools [evil] is folly [ivvelet].
22.notes: sekel (H7922), sound sense, is a maqor (H4726) -- a spring that never fails -- of chay (H2416) to its owner (ba'al, H1167). The contrast bites: what the fool (evil, H191) receives as musar (H4148), correction, only confirms his ivvelet (H200) -- folly is its own teacher and its own punishment, instructing him in nothing but more of itself.

23.text: The heart of the wise gives his mouth good sense and adds persuasion to his lips.
23.amp: The heart [leb] of the wise [chakam] teaches [sakal -- makes wise, gives insight to] his mouth [peh], and adds [yasaph -- increases] learning [leqach -- persuasive instruction] to his lips [saphah].
23.notes: the wise man's words begin upstream, in the leb (H3820), which makes his peh (H6310) wise (sakal, H7919; the KJV margin: 'maketh wise'). As in v.21, the heart's wisdom adds (yasaph, H3254) leqach (H3948) to the saphah (H8193) -- speech is the overflow of an instructed heart, never mere cleverness on the tongue (cf. Matt 12:34).

24.text: Gracious words are a honeycomb -- sweet to the soul and healing to the bones.
24.amp: Pleasant [no'am -- delightful, agreeable] words [emer] are as a honeycomb [tsuph -- the dripping comb of honey], sweet [matoq -- sweet to the taste] to the soul [nephesh], and health [marpe -- healing, a cure] to the bones [etsem].
24.notes: no'am (H5278) words are a tsuph (H6688) -- a honeycomb still oozing -- matoq (H4966), sweet to the nephesh (H5315), and marpe (H4832), medicine to the etsem (H6106), the very frame of the body. Kind speech nourishes and heals at once; cf. the bone-drying power of a crushed spirit (17:22). Words reach deeper than the ear.

25.text: There is a way that looks right to a man, but its end is the road to death.
25.amp: There is [yesh -- there exists] a way [derek] that seems right [yashar -- straight, upright] to a man [ish], but its end [acharit -- its outcome, what it finally comes to] is the ways [derek] of death [mavet].
25.notes: this proverb is grave enough to be repeated verbatim from 14:12. A derek (H1870) can look yashar (H3477) -- perfectly straight -- to the ish (H376) walking it, yet its acharit (H319), its final issue, is mavet (H4194). The eye that judged its own ways clean in v.2 is warned: self-evident rightness is no proof; only the LORD's verdict and the road's end tell the truth.

26.text: A laborer's appetite works on his behalf, for his hunger keeps driving him on.
26.amp: The appetite [nephesh -- the hungering soul, here the belly's craving] of him who labors [amel -- the toiler, the worker who suffers] labors [amal -- toils, works hard] for him; for his mouth [peh] craves [akaph -- presses, urges] it of him.
26.notes: a wry observation on the goad of need. The amel (H6001), the toiler, is driven by his own nephesh (H5315) -- here the appetite -- which amal (H5998), labors right alongside him; his peh (H6310), his hunger for bread, akaph (H404), presses him on (the KJV margin: 'boweth unto him'). Necessity itself, under God's design, becomes a spur to honest work.

27.text: A worthless man digs up trouble, and on his lips there is a scorching fire.
27.amp: An ungodly [beliyya'al -- worthlessness, wickedness; 'son of Belial'] man [ish] digs up [karah -- digs out, excavates] evil [ra], and in his lips [saphah] there is as a burning [tsarebet -- a scorching, a searing heat] fire [esh].
27.notes: beliyya'al (H1100) names utter worthlessness, later a name for the devil himself. Such a man karah (H3738), digs as for a pit or a buried thing, unearthing ra (H7451), mischief; and his saphah (H8193) carries esh (H784) that scorches (tsarebet, H6867). This gallery of evildoers (vv. 27-30) is marked above all by destructive speech (cf. Jas 3:6).

28.text: A perverse man scatters strife, and a whisperer divides the closest of friends.
28.amp: A perverse [tahpukah -- twisted, upside-down] man [ish] sows [shalach -- sends out, lets loose] strife [madon -- contention, quarreling], and a whisperer [nirgan -- a slanderer, a backbiting murmurer] separates [parad -- divides, drives apart] chief friends [alluph -- close companions, intimate friends].
28.notes: tahpukah (H8419) is speech and conduct turned upside down; such a man shalach (H7971), looses madon (H4066) like an arrow. Worse is the nirgan (H5372), the whisperer, whose quiet slander does what open quarrels cannot -- parad (H6504), to split apart, even an alluph (H441), a bosom friend (cf. 17:9; 18:8). Gossip is the most surgical of weapons.

29.text: A man of violence lures his neighbor and leads him down a road that is not good.
29.amp: A violent [chamas -- marked by violence, injustice, cruelty] man [ish] entices [pathah -- persuades, seduces, draws open] his neighbor [rea] and leads [yalak -- causes to walk, conducts] him into the way [derek] that is not good [tov].
29.notes: the man of chamas (H2555) -- the very violence that filled the earth before the flood (Gen 6:11) -- works first by pathah (H6601), the seducing persuasion of 1:10, drawing his rea (H7453) open. He then yalak (H3212), walks him down a derek (H1870) that is 'not good,' an understatement for the road to ruin. Evil recruits before it acts.

30.text: He who narrows his eyes is plotting perversities; he who purses his lips has already settled on evil.
30.amp: He who shuts [atsah -- squeezes shut, narrows] his eyes [ayin] to devise [chashab -- plan, scheme] perverse things [tahpukah -- twisted plots]; biting [qarats -- pinching, compressing] his lips [saphah], he brings to pass [kalah -- completes, accomplishes, brings to its end] evil [ra].
30.notes: the body betrays the scheming heart. atsah (H6095), squeezing the ayin (H5869) nearly shut, is the look of concentrated plotting (chashab, H2803) of tahpukah (H8419); qarats (H7169), pinching the saphah (H8193) tight, is the face of resolve. The doubled kalah (H3615) -- to finish, to consume -- says the evil is as good as done; the gesture is the verdict (cf. 6:13; 10:10).

31.text: Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is found along the road of righteousness.
31.amp: The hoary head [sebah -- gray hair, the whiteness of old age] is a crown [atarah -- a wreath, a royal diadem] of glory [tiphereth -- splendor, beauty, honor], if it be found [matsa -- attained, reached] in the way [derek] of righteousness [tsedaqah].
31.notes: sebah (H7872), the gray head of age, is an atarah (H5850) -- the same word for a king's crown -- of tiphereth (H8597), glory. But the honor is conditional: it is matsa (H4672), found, only along the derek of tsedaqah (H6666). Long life crowns a righteous walk; gray hair earned in folly is no crown at all (cf. 20:29; Lev 19:32).

32.text: Better the one slow to anger than the mighty warrior, and the man who rules his own spirit than one who takes a city.
32.amp: He who is slow [arek -- long, patient, 'long of nostrils'] to anger [aph -- nose, and so the heat of anger] is better [tov] than the mighty [gibbor -- the warrior, the strong man]; and he who rules [mashal -- governs, holds dominion over] his spirit [ruach] than he who takes [lakad -- captures, seizes] a city [ir].
32.notes: the Hebrew idiom for patience is arek aph (H750 + H639) -- 'long of nose,' slow to flare. Such a man is tov (H2896) above the gibbor (H1368), the battlefield hero; and to mashal (H4910) one's own ruach (H7307) is a greater conquest than to lakad (H3920) a fortified ir (H5892). The hardest city to take is the self (cf. 25:28; Jas 1:19).

33.text: Into the fold of the robe the lot is thrown, yet how it falls -- every verdict it renders -- the LORD alone determines.
33.amp: The lot [goral -- the lot, the portion assigned by casting] is cast [tul -- thrown, hurled] into the lap [cheq -- the bosom, the fold of the garment], but its whole disposing [mishpat -- the decision, the verdict it renders] is of the LORD [YHWH].
33.notes: the chapter ends where it began -- under God's hand. The goral (H1486) was tul (H2904), tossed into the cheq (H2436), the garment's fold, to settle disputes and inheritances by what looked like chance. Yet its every mishpat (H4941) -- its outcome, its verdict -- is from the LORD (H3068). Even what seems most random falls within His rule (cf. v.1; Acts 1:24-26). The sovereignty that opened the chapter closes it.
